hints: Focus on the shape of the melting point trend across a period, not just the individual values.
Notice the very high peak followed by a sharp fall, this is the giant covalent Group 14 element like silicon dropping to simple molecular P and S.
Count back from that peak, since silicon is Group 14, work back three places to find where Group 1 sodium must sit.
walkthrough:
**Recall the Period 3 melting point pattern**

Think of how melting point changes from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{S}$. It rises from $\text{Na}$ to $\text{Si}$ then falls sharply.

$$\text{Na (low) < Mg < Al < Si (giant peak) >> P, S (low)}$$

**Spot the silicon peak in the diagram**

The highest point is the 6th dot in the sequence. That huge peak can only be the giant covalent lattice with many strong covalent bonds.

That element is Group 14, like $\text{Si}$ in Period 3.

**Count back to find sodium**

Group 14 is 3 places after Group 1 in Period 3. So count back 3 from the peak: peak-1 is $\text{Al}$, peak-2 is $\text{Mg}$, peak-3 is $\text{Na}$.

$$\text{6th (Si) - 3 = 3rd point = C}$$

**Check the start fits**

If C is $\text{Na}$ (atomic number 11), then B is $\text{Ne}$ (10) and A is $\text{F}$ (9). That fits perfectly as $\text{F}$ is slightly higher than $\text{Ne}$, and both are very low as simple molecules.

options.A: A is too early. If C were later than sodium, A would be well before sodium. In fact A fits fluorine, a simple covalent molecule with very low melting point, not an alkali metal.
options.B: B is the lowest point just before the rise. This fits a noble gas like neon with only very weak instantaneous dipole forces. Sodium has metallic bonding and melts higher than this.
options.C: C is correct. It is three places before the giant covalent peak (silicon). That puts C in Group 1 as sodium, D as magnesium, next as aluminium, then silicon at the peak, followed by phosphorus and sulfur. The low A and B then fit fluorine and neon.
options.D: D is already high up the rising slope. This fits magnesium with stronger metallic bonding (2+ ions, more delocalised electrons) than sodium. Sodium must be lower and earlier, at C.
